questions.question: Masakhane Traders owes Siyakha Wholesalers R33 400 per its ledger, but Siyakha's statement shows R52 900. Differences: an unrecorded invoice of R5 800 for delivered goods; a payment of R7 600 made after the statement date; a granted discount of R850 not yet processed; a debit note of R1 750 for returns not yet credited; and an invoice of R3 500 belonging to another customer. Complete the reconciliation and state the amount to pay.
questions.expected_answer: Assign each difference to the record that is behind or wrong. Ledger side: add the R5 800 invoice — the goods are real and the ledger must catch up — giving 33 400 plus 5 800, R39 200. Statement side: subtract the R7 600 payment the statement could not have seen, the R850 discount not yet processed, the R1 750 return not yet credited, and the R3 500 posting error belonging to another customer — 52 900 less 13 700, R39 200. Both records now agree at R39 200, which is the true debt, the figure for trade payables, and the amount to pay. Paying the raw statement would have cost R13 700 too much, including R3 500 of someone else's goods — the rule is never pay a statement, pay a reconciled statement.

questions.question: Masakhane's debtors' book of R96 000, on 30-day terms, ages as: current R48 000, thirty days R24 000, sixty days R14 400, ninety-plus days R9 600. Interpret the analysis and set out the business's response, including prevention.
questions.expected_answer: Percentages first: 50 percent current, 25 percent at thirty days, 15 percent at sixty and 10 percent at ninety-plus. Seventy-five percent is within terms, but 25 percent — R24 000 — is overdue, and R9 600 has been owed three months or more. Old debt is sick debt: recovery likelihood falls steeply with age, so the ninety-day column is where bad debts are born and where the provision for bad debts should look. The overdue book must also be financed — collecting slowly while paying suppliers on time makes the business an unwilling bank, possibly at overdraft rates. Response in escalating order: statements and reminders; interest on overdue amounts if the credit agreement allows; suspension of further credit; then collection or attorneys where the debt justifies the cost. Prevention beats collection: credit checks before accounts open, credit limits enforced, and immediate invoicing. Watched over time, the percentage drift is an early-warning system — a book sliding from seventy-five percent within terms toward fifty is credit control failing before a single write-off.

questions.question: Explain how the bank reconciliation exposes rolling of cash, how paying unreconciled statements invites invoice fraud, and the segregation principle that underlies all reconciliation controls.
questions.expected_answer: Rolling of cash: a cashier keeps a day's takings and banks the next day's receipts under the earlier date, covering the hole forward forever. The daily records look perfect; the reconciliation shows the fingerprint — deposits always landing a beat late, or a deposit outstanding for weeks. The theft is complete on day one; the rolling only hides it, and comparing deposit dates in the cash journal with the bank statement exposes it. Invoice fraud: businesses that pay statement totals without reconciling will eventually pay for goods never delivered — fictitious invoices flow toward whoever never checks — so payments require three-way matching of order, delivery note and invoice, with the reconciliation catching what slips through. The underlying principle: segregation plus an independent eye — the person who handles the asset must not keep its record, the record-keeper must not prepare the reconciliation, and someone senior must actually review it, because a reconciliation nobody reads is a lock nobody turns. Late payment carries its own price even without fraud: interest, lost discounts and a damaged credit rating, which is why paying on the last day within terms is treasury discipline.
